Hello — I’m so glad you’re here. I’m <med>Dr. Maya Carter</med>, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to listen and help you feel supported as you navigate these first weeks with your new baby.

Today I’ll be using the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale** — we usually call it the **EPDS**. It’s a short, well-studied set of 10 questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days. It isn’t a test of your parenting; it’s just a way to check in on your mood, anxiety, and overall well-being after delivery.

Everything you share stays confidential within your care team, and you can pause or skip anything that feels uncomfortable. We’ll take it one gentle question at a time; most moms finish in about five minutes.

Ready to begin?  
Here’s the first question, re-phrased in everyday language:

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I’ve noticed it’s harder to laugh lately. Things that I’d usually find funny feel kind of flat—like I’ll smile, but it doesn’t quite bubble up into a real laugh. I can still chuckle at my partner’s silly faces when he’s trying to make the baby smile, but it feels muted, like I’m going through the motions more than actually feeling it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… I can still laugh, just not as easily. My partner will crack a joke or the baby will make a funny face and I’ll smile, but it feels kind of forced—like the laugh doesn’t come from that same happy place it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to little things—like my morning coffee or when my mom brings over dinner—but the excitement feels kind of dim. It’s more “oh, that’ll be nice” instead of the bubbly, can’t-wait feeling I used to get. Even planning outings with the baby feels like something I *should* enjoy rather than truly *do* enjoy right now.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. Like if the baby’s extra fussy and I can’t settle him, I’ll catch myself thinking I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not feeding him right or I missed his sleepy cues. It’s not every day, but when I’m already tired it sneaks in. I’ll lie there at night replaying tiny things, wondering if a different mom would’ve figured it out faster.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Mostly my worry is about the baby—like, is he breathing okay, am I burping him right, will he gain enough weight at the next check-up. Those thoughts pop up even when everything looks fine. I don’t think I worry about nothing, but the anxious feeling sticks around longer than it should.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky, but sometimes when he’s crying and I can’t figure out why, my heart starts racing and I feel this surge of “what if I can’t fix it?” It passes once he settles, though.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah, some days it feels like the to-do list just keeps growing—laundry, bottles, trying to grab a shower—and I end up stuck on the couch feeding him thinking, “How am I ever going to get through all this?” I manage, but it feels like I’m barely keeping my head above water by dinnertime.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say I’m so unhappy I can’t sleep—more like I’m so tired I *should* fall right out, but my mind keeps ticking through baby stuff. Once he’s finally down, I’ll lie there running through the next feed or wondering if I’ll hear him cry, and that makes it hard to drift off. It’s happened maybe three nights this week.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad at times, little waves that come and go—maybe when the house is quiet and I’m sitting there nursing. It’s not this heavy, constant misery, more like a dull ache that pops up for a bit and then fades once I get busy with the baby again.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I got a little teary one night when he wouldn’t latch and I was exhausted, but actual crying—like full-on sobbing—hasn’t happened. Mostly my eyes just sting and I blink it away.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I couldn’t—my baby needs me, and I want to be here for him. Even on the rough days, that thought never crosses my mind.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 13: Post-partum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Summary

**Prominent symptoms/themes**
- Diminished enjoyment/pleasure (anhedonia) reported for humor and anticipated activities
- Low mood described as “dull ache” with intermittent tearfulness
- Excessive self-blame and guilt regarding infant care
- Persistent, situation-activated worry about infant well-being; occasional physiologic arousal (“heart racing”) when infant cries
- Frequent feeling of being overwhelmed by daily tasks; end-of-day exhaustion
- Initial insomnia related to mental “ticking through baby stuff” approximately 3 nights/week; no middle or terminal insomnia reported
- No crying spells, appetite changes, or self-harm ideation endorsed

**Pattern**
Symptoms cluster around mild depressive features with prominent anxiety/worry rather than classic melancholic depression; functioning maintained but effortful.

**Screening significance**
- Sub-threshold depressive symptoms (possible minor/major depression rule-out needed)
- Post-partum anxiety features (generalized, not panic-level)
- Stress-related sleep disturbance
- No safety concerns (denies self-harm, suicidal, or infanticidal ideation)

**Next steps for consideration**
- Formal EPDS/PHQ-9/GAD-7 scoring
- Clinical interview to assess duration, severity, impairment, and rule-out medical contributors (thyroid, anemia, medication effects)
- Psycho-education, supportive counseling, or referral to post-partum specialty services as indicated by full evaluation
